drills.q: Distinguish pipelining from out-of-order execution, and state whether you can have one without the other.
drills.a: Pipelining overlaps instruction stages but keeps program order; OoO lets independent instructions execute in a different order, retiring via a ROB in original order. Pipelining without OoO is the classic in-order 5-stage RISC pipeline (common in simple/embedded cores); OoO without pipelining is essentially never built since OoO's benefit compounds with pipelining's overlap.

drills.q: Name the three classic pipeline hazard types and a concrete fix for each.
drills.a: Structural (two instructions want the same resource -- duplicate resources, e.g. separate I/D caches, multiple ALU ports), data (an instruction needs a value not yet produced -- forwarding for close ALU deps, OoO scheduling/stall for load-use), control (branch target unknown -- predict + speculative execution, squash-and-refetch on misprediction).

drills.q: Why can't forwarding fully eliminate a load-use hazard the way it eliminates an ALU-to-ALU dependency?
drills.a: Forwarding routes an already-computed value from one stage's output to another's input; an ALU result exists at end of EX and can forward immediately. A load's result doesn't exist until MEM completes (L1 hit latency ~4-5 cycles), so an instruction consuming it right away has nothing yet to forward -- it stalls, or OoO execution hides the wait with unrelated independent work.

drills.q: Estimate the rough throughput cost of a 2% branch misprediction rate on a 19-stage pipeline with one branch per ~5-6 instructions, given a ~15-20 cycle misprediction penalty.
drills.a: Roughly 1 misprediction per 250-300 instructions, each costing ~15-20 cycles versus ~1 cycle those instructions would otherwise take -- a back-of-envelope estimate puts the overhead in the single-digit percent range of total cycles, directly visible as reduced IPC in perf stat.

drills.q: What is a reorder buffer, why does its size matter, and give rough entry counts for two current designs.
drills.a: The ROB tracks in-flight instructions in original program order so results retire in order despite OoO execution; its size bounds the instruction window the core can search past a stall (e.g. a cache-missing load) for independent work. Golden Cove ~512 entries, Zen4 ~320 entries -- both grown substantially as memory latency became the dominant bottleneck for many workloads.

drills.q: Explain register renaming and the specific hazard class it eliminates that forwarding does not address.
drills.a: Renaming maps the small architectural register set onto a much larger physical register file, giving every write a fresh physical register. This eliminates WAW/WAR false dependencies -- collisions that exist only because two unrelated instructions reuse the same register name, not because data actually flows between them. Forwarding instead addresses true read-after-write dependencies.

drills.q: Explain Spectre mechanically: how does speculative execution leak data despite architectural squash discarding the mispredicted instructions?
drills.a: An attacker mistrains a branch predictor so the core speculatively executes past a check it should have failed, performing a memory read using attacker-influenced data as an index, followed by an access dependent on that read's value. Architectural squash discards registers/memory writes but not microarchitectural state like cache lines pulled in during the speculative read -- the attacker measures cache-access timing afterward to infer which line was touched, reconstructing the leaked value without ever architecturally reading it.

drills.q: A hot reduction loop (sum += arr[i]) shows IPC ~1.0 on a 4+ wide core with all data L1-resident. Diagnose and fix, and note the numerical caveat.
drills.a: A single running accumulator creates a strict serial dependency chain -- each add waits on the previous add's result, so only one addition is ever in flight regardless of core width. Fix: use multiple independent partial-sum accumulators (or let SIMD lanes act as independent accumulators), summing at the end. Caveat: floating-point addition isn't associative, so this changes rounding behavior versus strict left-to-right summation -- not purely free, especially with widely differing magnitudes.

drills.q: When is it acceptable to disable Spectre/Meltdown mitigations for performance, and when is it a red flag?
drills.a: Only defensible when the threat model genuinely excludes the attack surface closed by mitigations -- e.g. a single-tenant, physically isolated batch node running fully trusted code with no untrusted co-tenants or code execution -- and even then as a deliberate, documented decision. It is a red flag on any multi-tenant or shared infrastructure (e.g. Kubernetes nodes with multiple tenants' pods), since that is exactly the scenario the mitigations exist to protect, structurally identical to recommending tcp_tw_recycle for TIME_WAIT.

drills.q: A numeric loop over a large float array shows low IPC and high cache-miss rate under perf stat. Does adding wider SIMD (AVX2 to AVX-512) help, and why or why not?
drills.a: No, or only marginally -- if the loop is memory-bandwidth-bound (confirmed via high cache-miss rate and low IPC despite simple arithmetic), the ALUs are already waiting on data; widening SIMD moves the same total bytes in wider chunks per instruction but doesn't relieve a bandwidth bottleneck. Wider SIMD pays off on compute-bound kernels with more arithmetic per byte loaded (e.g. FMA-heavy inner loops), not bandwidth-bound ones -- profile before concluding an ISA feature doesn't help.
